entries.0bfd9d9a4b81a2284f188234037245e70e70ff88: <div sID="gen20218" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="8" osisID="Amos.8" sID="Amos.8"/> <div eID="gen20218" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20219" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen20220" type="x-p"/> Sinful times are here attended with sorrowful times, so necessary is the connexion between them; it is threatened here again and again that the laughter shall be turned into mourning. I. By the vision of "basket of summer-fruit" is signified the hastening on of the ruin threatened (<reference osisRef="Amos.8.1-Amos.8.3">ver. 1-3</reference>) and that shall change their note. II. Oppressors are here called to an account for their abusing the poor; and their destruction is foretold, which will set them a mourning, <reference osisRef="Amos.8.4-Amos.8.10">ver. 4-10</reference>. III. A famine of the word of God is here made the punishment of a people that go a whoring after other gods (<reference osisRef="Amos.8.11-Amos.8.14">ver. 11-14</reference>); yet for this, which is the most mournful judgment of all, they are not here brought in mourning.
entries.9e368a71e2988ac724b610527e777c2e4dfb4015: <div eID="gen20220" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen20219" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Vision of Summer Fruit. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 785.)</title> <div sID="gen20221" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Thus hath the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> shewed unto me: and behold a basket of summer fruit. <hi type="super">2</hi> And he said, Amos, what seest thou? And I said, A basket of summer fruit. Then said the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> unto me, The end is come upon my people of Israel; I will not again pass by them any more. <hi type="super">3</hi> And the songs of the temple shall be howlings in that day, saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> : <hi type="italic">there shall be</hi> many dead bodies in every place; they shall cast <hi type="italic">them</hi> forth with silence. <div eID="gen20221" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20222" type="x-p"/> The great reason why sinners defer their repentance <hi type="italic">de die in diem—from day to day,</hi> is because they think God thus defers his judgments, and there is no song wherewith they so effectually sing themselves asleep as that, <hi type="italic">My Lord delays his coming;</hi> and therefore God, by his prophets, frequently represents to Israel the day of his wrath not only as just and certain, but as very near and hastening on apace; so he does in these verses. <div eID="gen20222" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20223" type="x-p"/> I. The approach of the threatened ruin is represented by <hi type="italic">a basket of summer-fruit</hi> which Amos saw in vision; for the Lord <hi type="italic">showed it</hi> to him (<reference osisRef="Amos.8.1">v. 1</reference>) and obliged him to take notice of it (<reference osisRef="Amos.8.2">v. 2</reference>): <hi type="italic">Amos, what seest thou?</hi> Note, It concerns us to enquire whether we do indeed see that which God has been pleased to show us, and hear what he has been pleased to say to us; for many a thing God speaks, God shows <hi type="italic">once, yea twice,</hi> and men <hi type="italic">perceive it not.</hi> Are we in the midst of the visions of the Almighty? Let us consider what we see. He saw <hi type="italic">a basket of summer-fruit</hi> gathered and ready to be eaten, which signified, 1. That they were ripe for destruction, rotten ripe, and it was time for God to put in the sickle of his judgments and to cut them off; nay, the thing was in effect done already, and they lay ready to be eaten up. 2. That the year of God's patience was drawing towards a conclusion; it was autumn with them, and their year would quickly have its period in a dismal winter. 3. Those we call <hi type="italic">summer-fruits</hi> that will not keep till winter, but must be used immediately, an emblem of this people, that had nothing solid or consistent in them. <div eID="gen20223" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20224" type="x-p"/> II. The intent and meaning of this vision is no more than this: It signifies that <hi type="italic">the end has come upon my people Israel.</hi> The word that signifies <hi type="italic">the end</hi> is <hi type="italic">ketz,</hi> which is of near affinity with <hi type="italic">kitz,</hi> the word used for <hi type="italic">summer-fruit.</hi> God has long spared them, and borne with them, but now his patience is tired out; they are indeed <hi type="italic">his people Israel,</hi> but their end, that <hi type="italic">latter end</hi> they have been so often reminded of, but have so long forgotten, has now come. Note, If sinners do not make an end of sin, God will make an end of them, yea though they be <hi type="italic">his people Israel.</hi> What was said <reference osisRef="Amos.7.8">ch. vii. 8</reference> is here repeated as God's determined resolution, <hi type="italic">I will not again pass by them any more;</hi> they shall not be connived at as they have been, nor the judgment coming turned away. <div eID="gen20224" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20225" type="x-p"/> III. The consequence of this shall be a universal desolation (<reference osisRef="Amos.8.3">v. 3</reference>): When <hi type="italic">the end</hi> shall come sorrow and death shall ride in triumph; they are accustomed to go together, and shall at length go away together, when in heaven <hi type="italic">there shall be no more death, nor sorrow,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.21.4">Rev. xxi. 4</reference>. But here in a sinful world, in a sinful nation, 1. Sorrow reigns, reigns to such a degree that <hi type="italic">the songs of the temple shall be howlings</hi>—the songs of God's temple at Jerusalem, or rather of their idol-temples, where they used, when, in honour of the golden calves, they had <hi type="italic">eaten and drunk,</hi> to <hi type="italic">rise up to play.</hi> They were perhaps wanton profane songs; and it is certain that sooner or later those will be turned into howlings. Or, if they had a sound and show of piety and religion, yet, not coming from the heart, nor being sung to the glory of God, he valued them not, but would justly turn them into howlings. Note, Mourning will follow sinful mirth, yea, and sacred mirth too, it if be not sincere. And, when God's judgments are abroad, they will soon turn the greatest joy into the greatest heaviness, the temple-songs, which used to sound so pleasantly, not only into sighs and groans, but into loud howlings, which sound dismally. They shall come to the temple, and, finding that in ruins, there they shall howl most bitterly. 2. Death reigns, reigns to such a degree that there shall be <hi type="italic">dead bodies, many</hi> dead bodies <hi type="italic">in every place</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.110.6">Ps. cx. 6</reference>), slain by sword or pestilence, so many that the survivors shall not bury them with the usual pomp and solemnity of funerals; they shall not so much as have the bell tolled, but they shall <hi type="italic">cast them forth with silence,</hi> shall bury them in the dead of the night, and charge all about them to be silent and to take notice of it, either because they have not wherewithal to bear the charges of a funeral, or because, the killing disease being infectious, none will come near them, or for fear the enemy should be provoked, if they should be known to lament their slain. Or they shall charge themselves and one another silently to submit to the hand of God in these desolating judgments, and not to repine and quarrel with him. Or it may be taken not for a patient, but a sullen silence; their hearts shall be hardened, and all these judgments shall not extort from them one word of acknowledgment either of God's righteousness or their own unrighteousness.
entries.fc5cbd9ad7ec2acce61adcf7b6e488bd25373e8f: <div eID="gen20225" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Sin and Doom of Oppressors. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 785.)</title> <div sID="gen20226" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">4</hi> Hear this, O ye that swallow up the needy, even to make the poor of the land to fail, <hi type="super">5</hi> Saying, When will the new moon be gone, that we may sell corn? and the sabbath, that we may set forth wheat, making the ephah small, and the shekel great, and falsifying the balances by deceit? <hi type="super">6</hi> That we may buy the poor for silver, and the needy for a pair of shoes; <hi type="italic">yea,</hi> and sell the refuse of the wheat? <hi type="super">7</hi> The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath sworn by the excellency of Jacob, Surely I will never forget any of their works. <hi type="super">8</hi> Shall not the land tremble for this, and every one mourn that dwelleth therein? and it shall rise up wholly as a flood; and it shall be cast out and drowned, as <hi type="italic">by</hi> the flood of Egypt. <hi type="super">9</hi> And it shall come to pass in that day, saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> , that I will cause the sun to go down at noon, and I will darken the earth in the clear day: <hi type="super">10</hi> And I will turn your feasts into mourning, and all your songs into lamentation; and I will bring up sackcloth upon all loins, and baldness upon every head; and I will make it as the mourning of an only <hi type="italic">son,</hi> and the end thereof as a bitter day. <div eID="gen20226" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20227" type="x-p"/> God is here contending with proud oppressors, and showing them, <div eID="gen20227" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20228" type="x-p"/> I. The heinousness of the sin they were guilty of; in short, they had the character of the unjust judge (<reference osisRef="Luke.18.2">Luke xviii. 2</reference>) that neither <hi type="italic">feared God</hi> nor <hi type="italic">regarded man.</hi> <div eID="gen20228" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20229" type="x-p"/> 1. Observe them in their devotions, and you will say, "They had no reverence for God." Bad as they are, they do indeed keep up a show and form of godliness; they observe the <hi type="italic">sabbath</hi> and the <hi type="italic">new moon;</hi> they put some difference between those days and other days, but they were soon weary of them, and had no affection at all to them, for their hearts were wholly set upon the world and the things of it. It is a sad character which this gives of them, that they said, <hi type="italic">When will the sabbath be gone, that we may sell corn?</hi> Yet is still the character of many that are called Christians. (1.) They were weary of sabbath days. "When will they be <hi type="italic">gone?</hi>" They were weary of the restraints of the sabbaths and the new-moons, and wished them over because they might <hi type="italic">do no servile work therein.</hi> They were weary of the work or business of the sabbaths and new-moons, snuffed at it (<reference osisRef="Mal.1.13">Mal. i. 13</reference>), and were, as <hi type="italic">Doeg, detained before the Lord</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Sam.21.7">1 Sam. xxi. 7</reference>); they would rather have been any where else than about God's altars. Note, Sabbath days and sabbath work are a burden to carnal hearts, that are always afraid of doing too much for God and eternity. Can we spend our time better than in communication with God? And how much time do we spend pleasantly with the world? Will not the sabbath be gone before we have done the work of it and reaped the gains of it? Why then should we be in such haste to part with it? (2.) They were fond of market-days: they longed to be <hi type="italic">selling corn</hi> and <hi type="italic">setting forth wheat.</hi> When they were employed in religious services they were thinking of their marketings; their hearts <hi type="italic">went after their covetousness</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.33.31">Ezek. xxxiii. 31</reference>), and thus made my Father's house a house of merchandise, nay, a den of thieves. They were weary of holy duties because their worldly business stood still the while; in this they were as in their element, but in God's sanctuary as a fish upon dry ground. Note, Those are strangers to God, and enemies to themselves, that love market days better than sabbath days, that would rather be selling corn than worshipping God. <div eID="gen20229" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20230" type="x-p"/> 2. Observe them in their conversations, and you will see they have no regard to man; and this commonly follows upon the former; those that have lost the savour of piety will not long retain the sense of common honesty. They neither <hi type="italic">do justly</hi> nor <hi type="italic">love mercy.</hi> (1.) They cheat those they deal with. When they <hi type="italic">sell their corn</hi> they impose upon the buyer, both in giving out the goods and in receiving the money for them. They measure him the corn by their own measure, and pretend to give him what he agreed for, but they <hi type="italic">make the ephah small.</hi> The measure is scanty, and not statute-measure, and so they wrong him that way. When they receive his money they must weigh fit in their own scales, by their own weights, and the <hi type="italic">shekel</hi> they weigh by is above standard: <hi type="italic">They make the shekel great,</hi> so that the money, being found too light, must have more added to it; and so they cheat that way too, and this under colour and pretence of exactness in doing justice. By such wicked practices as these men show such a greediness of the world, such a love of themselves, such a contempt of mankind in general, of the particular persons they deal with, and of the sacred laws of justice, as prove them to have in their hearts neither the fear nor the love of that God who has so plainly said that <hi type="italic">false weights and balances are an abomination to him.</hi> Another instance of their fraudulent dealing is that they <hi type="italic">sell the refuse of the wheat,</hi> and, taking advantage of their neighbour's ignorance or necessity, make them take it at the same price at which they sell the <hi type="italic">finest of the wheat.</hi> (2.) They are barbarous and unmerciful to the poor: <hi type="italic">They swallow up the needy,</hi> and <hi type="italic">make the poor of the land to fail.</hi> [1.] They valued themselves so much on their wealth that they looked upon all that were poor with the highest contempt imaginable; they hated them, could not endure them, but abandoned them, and therefore did what they could to make them cease, not by relieving them to make them cease to be poor, but by banishing and destroying them to make them cease to be, or at least to be in their land. But he who thus <hi type="italic">reproaches the poor despises his Maker,</hi> in whose hands <hi type="italic">rich and poor meet together.</hi> [2.] They were so eager to increase their wealth, and make it more, that they robbed the poor to enrich themselves; and they fastened upon the poor, to <hi type="italic">make a prey</hi> of them, because they were not able to obtain any redress nor to resist or revenge the violence of their oppressors. Those riches that are got by the ruin of the poor will bring ruin on those that get them. They swallowed up the poor by making them hard bargains, and cheating them in those bargains; for <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> they <hi type="italic">falsify the balances by deceit,</hi> not only that they <hi type="italic">may enrich themselves,</hi> may have money at command, and so may have every thing else (as they think) at command too, but that they may impoverish those about them, and bring them so low that they may force them to become slaves to them, and so, having drained them of every thing else, they may have their labour for nothing, or next to nothing. Thus <hi type="italic">they buy the poor for silver;</hi> they bring them and their <hi type="italic">children into bondage,</hi> because they have not wherewithal to pay for the corn they have bought; see <reference osisRef="Neh.5.2-Neh.5.5">Neh. v. 2-5</reference>. And there were so many that they were reduced to this extremity that the price was very low; and the oppressors had beaten it down so that you might buy a poor man to be your slave <hi type="italic">for a pair of shoes.</hi> Property was first invaded and then liberty; it is the method of oppressors first to make men beggars and then to make them their vassals. Thus is the dignity of the human nature lost in the misery of those that are trampled on and the tenderness of it in the sin of those that trample on them. <div eID="gen20230" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20231" type="x-p"/> II. The grievousness of the punishment that shall be inflicted on them for this sin. When the poor are injured they will <hi type="italic">cry unto God,</hi> and he will hear their cry, and reckon with those that are injurious to them, for, they being his receivers, he takes the wrongs done to them as done to himself, <reference osisRef="Exod.22.23-Exod.22.24">Exod. xxii. 23, 24</reference>. <div eID="gen20231" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20232" type="x-p"/> 1. God will remember their sin against them: <hi type="italic">He has sworn by the excellency of Jacob</hi> (<reference osisRef="Amos.8.7">v. 7</reference>), by himself, for he can swear by no greater; and who but he is the glory and magnificence of Jacob? He has sworn by those tokens of his presence with them, and his favour to them, which they had profaned and abused, and had done what they could to make them detestable to him; for he is said (<reference osisRef="Amos.6.8">ch. vi. 8</reference>) to <hi type="italic">abhor the excellency of Jacob.</hi> He swears <hi type="italic">in his wrath,</hi> swears by his own name, that name which was so well known and was so great in Israel. He swears, <hi type="italic">Surely I will never forget any of their works,</hi> but upon all occasions they shall be remembered against them, for more is implied than is expressed. <hi type="italic">I will never forget them</hi> is as much as to say, <hi type="italic">I will never forgive them;</hi> and then it proclaims the case of these unjust unmerciful men to be miserable indeed, eternally miserable; woe, and a thousand woes, to that man that is cut off by an oath of God from all benefit by pardoning mercy; and those have reason to fear judgment without mercy that have <hi type="italic">shown no mercy.</hi> <div eID="gen20232" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20233" type="x-p"/> 2. He will bring utter ruin and confusion upon them. It is here described largely, and in a great variety of emphatic expressions, that, if possible, they might be frightened into a sincere repentance and reformation. (1.) There shall be a universal terror and consternation: <hi type="italic">Shall not the land tremble for this</hi> (<reference osisRef="Amos.8.8">v. 8</reference>), <hi type="italic">this land,</hi> out of which you thought to drive the poor? <hi type="italic">Shall not every one mourn that dwells therein?</hi> Certainly he shall. Note, Those that will not tremble and mourn as they ought for national sins shall be made to tremble and mourn for national judgments; those that look without concern upon the sins of the oppressors, which should make them tremble, and upon the miseries of the oppressed, which should them mourn, God will find out a way to make them tremble at the fury of those that oppress them and mourn for their own losses and sufferings by it. (2.) There shall be a universal deluge and desolation. When God comes forth against them the waters of trouble and calamity shall <hi type="italic">rise up wholly as a flood,</hi> that swells, when it is dammed up, and soon overflows its banks. Every thing shall make against them. That with which they thought to check the progress of God's judgments shall but make them rise the higher. Judgments shall force their way as the <hi type="italic">breaking forth of waters.</hi> The whole land <hi type="italic">shall be cast out, and drowned,</hi> and laid under water, as the land of Egypt is every year by the overflowing of its river Nile. Or the expressions may allude to some former judgments of God. Their ruin <hi type="italic">shall rise up wholly as a flood,</hi> as Noah's flood, which overwhelmed the whole world, so shall this the whole land; and the land shall be <hi type="italic">cast out, and drowned, as by the flood of Egypt,</hi> as Pharaoh and his Egyptians were buried in the Red Sea, which was to them the <hi type="italic">flood of Egypt,</hi> both which judgments, as this which is here threatened, were the punishment of violence and oppression, which the Lord is the avenger of. <div eID="gen20233" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20234" type="x-p"/> 3. It shall surprise them, and come upon them when they little think of it (<reference osisRef="Amos.8.9">v. 9</reference>): "<hi type="italic">I will cause the sun to go down at noon,</hi> when it is in its full strength and lustre, at their noon, when they promise themselves a long afternoon, and think they have at least half a day good before them. The <hi type="italic">earth</hi> shall be <hi type="italic">darkened in the clear day,</hi> when every thing looks pleasant and hopeful." Thus uncertain are all our creature-comforts and enjoyments, even life itself; the highest degree of health and prosperity often proves the next degree to sickness and adversity; Job's sun <hi type="italic">went down at noon;</hi> many are taken away in the midst of their days, and their sun goes down at noon. In the midst of life we are in death. Thus <hi type="italic">terrible</hi> are the judgments of God to those that sleep in security; they are to them as the sun's <hi type="italic">going down at noon;</hi> the less they are expected the more confounding they are. When they <hi type="italic">cry Peace and safety</hi> then <hi type="italic">sudden destruction</hi> comes, comes <hi type="italic">as a snare,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.21.35">Luke xxi. 35</reference>. <div eID="gen20234" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20235" type="x-p"/> 4. It shall change their note, and mar all their mirth (<reference osisRef="Amos.8.10">v. 10</reference>): <hi type="italic">I will turn your feasts into mourning,</hi> as (<reference osisRef="Amos.8.3">v. 3</reference>) the <hi type="italic">songs of the temple into howlings.</hi> Note, The end of the sinner's mirth and jollity is heaviness. As <hi type="italic">to the upright there arises light in the darkness,</hi> which gives them <hi type="italic">the oil of joy for mourning,</hi> so on the wicked there falls darkness in the midst of light, which turns their <hi type="italic">laughter into mourning,</hi> their <hi type="italic">joy into heaviness.</hi> So great, so general, shall the desolation be, that <hi type="italic">sackcloth shall be brought upon all loins, and baldness upon every head,</hi> instead of the <hi type="italic">well-set hair</hi> and the rich garments they used to wear. The mourning at that day shall be as <hi type="italic">mourning for an only son,</hi> which denotes the most bitter and lasting lamentation. But are there then no hopes that when things are at the worst they will mend, and that at evening time it will yet be light? No, even <hi type="italic">the end thereof shall be as a bitter day,</hi> a day of bitter mourning; that state of impenitent sinners grows worse and worse, and the last of all will be the worst of all. <hi type="italic">This shall you have at my hand, you shall lie down in sorrow.</hi>
entries.a7eb70e1c9b9628e7b4334734e1bb3c847b02d85: <div eID="gen20235" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Spiritual Famine Threatened; Judgments Threatened. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 785.)</title> <div sID="gen20236" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">11</hi> Behold, the days come, saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> , that I will send a famine in the land, not a famine of bread, nor a thirst for water, but of hearing the words of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : <hi type="super">12</hi> And they shall wander from sea to sea, and from the north even to the east, they shall run to and fro to seek the word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and shall not find <hi type="italic">it.</hi> <hi type="super">13</hi> In that day shall the fair virgins and young men faint for thirst. <hi type="super">14</hi> They that swear by the sin of Samaria, and say, Thy god, O Dan, liveth; and, The manner of Beer-sheba liveth; even they shall fall, and never rise up again. <div eID="gen20236" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20237" type="x-p"/> In these verses is threatened, <div eID="gen20237" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20238" type="x-p"/> I. A general judgment of spiritual famine coming upon the whole land, a <hi type="italic">famine of the word of God,</hi> the failing of oracles and the scarcity of good preaching. This is spoken of as a thing at some distance: <hi type="italic">The days come,</hi> they will come hereafter, when another kind of darkness shall come upon that land of light. When Amos prophesied, and for a considerable time after, they had great plenty of prophets, abundant opportunities of <hi type="italic">hearing the word of God,</hi> in season and out of season; they had precept upon precept and line upon line; prophecy was their daily bread; and it is probable that they surfeited upon it, as Israel on the manna, and therefore God threatens that hereafter he will deprive them of this privilege. Probably in the land of Israel there were not so many prophets, about the time that their destruction came upon them, as there were in the land of Judah; and when the ten tribes went into captivity they <hi type="italic">saw not their signs,</hi> there were <hi type="italic">no more any prophets,</hi> none to <hi type="italic">show them how long,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.74.9">Ps. lxxiv. 9</reference>. The Jewish church, after Malachi, had no prophets for many ages; and some think this threatening looks further yet, to the blindness which has in part happened to Israel in the days of the Messiah, and the veil that is on the heart of the unbelieving Jews. They reject the gospel, and the ministers of it that God sends to them, and covet to have prophets of their own, as their fathers had, but they shall have none, <hi type="italic">the kingdom of God</hi> being <hi type="italic">taken from them</hi> and <hi type="italic">given to another people.</hi> Observe here, <div eID="gen20238" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20239" type="x-p"/> 1. What the judgment itself is that is threatened. It is a famine, a scarcity, not of bread and water (which are the necessary support of the body, and the want of which is very grievous), but a much sorer judgment than that, even a <hi type="italic">famine of hearing the words of the Lord.</hi> There shall be no congregations for ministers to preach to, nor any ministers to preach, nor any instructions and abilities given to those that do set up for preachers, to fit them for their work. The <hi type="italic">word of the Lord</hi> shall be <hi type="italic">precious</hi> and scarce; there shall be no <hi type="italic">vision,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.3.1">1 Sam. iii. 1</reference>. They shall have the written word, Bibles to read, but no ministers to explain and apply it to them, the water in the well, but nothing to draw with. It is a gracious promise (<reference osisRef="Isa.30.20">Isa. xxx. 20</reference>) that though they have a scarcity of bread they shall have plenty of the means of grace. God will <hi type="italic">give them the bread of adversity and the water of affliction,</hi> but their eyes shall see their teachers; and it was a common saying among the Puritans that brown bread and the gospel are good fare. But it is here a threatening that on the contrary they should have plenty enough of bread and water, and yet their teachers should be removed. Now, (1.) This was the departure of a great part of their glory from their land. This made their nation great and high, that <hi type="italic">to them were committed the oracles of God;</hi> but, when these were taken from them, their beauty was stained and their honour laid in the dust. (2.) This was a token of God's highest displeasure against them. Surely he was angry indeed with them when he would no more speak to them as he had done, and had abandoned them to ruin when he would no more afford them the means of bringing them to repentance. (3.) This made all the other calamities that were upon them truly melancholy, that they had no prophets to instruct and comfort them from the word of God, nor to give them any hopeful prospect. We should say at any time, and shall say in a time of trouble, that a famine of the word of God is the sorest famine, the heaviest judgment. <div eID="gen20239" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20240" type="x-p"/> 2. What will be the effect of this (<reference osisRef="Amos.8.12">v. 12</reference>): <hi type="italic">They shall wander from sea to sea,</hi> from the sea of Tiberias to the Great Sea, from one border of the country to another, to see if God will send them prophets, either by sea or land, from other countries; since they have none among themselves, they shall go from the <hi type="italic">north to the east;</hi> when they are disappointed in one place they shall try another, and shall <hi type="italic">run to and fro,</hi> as men at a loss, and in a hot pursuit to <hi type="italic">seek the word of the Lord,</hi> to enquire if there be any prophets, any prophecy, any message from God, but they <hi type="italic">shall not find it.</hi> (1.) Though to many this is no affliction at all, yet some will be very sensible of it as a great grievance, and will gladly travel far to hear a good sermon; but they shall sensibly feel the loss of those mercies which others have foolishly sinned away. (2.) Even those that slighted prophets when they had them shall wish for them as Saul did for Samuel, when they are deprived of them. Many never know the worth of mercies till they feel the want of them. Or it may be meant thus, Though they should thus wander from sea to sea, in quest of the word of God, yet shall they not find it. Note, The means of grace are moveable things; and the candlestick, when we think it stands most firmly, may be removed out of its place (<reference osisRef="Rev.2.5">Rev. ii. 5</reference>); and those that now slight the <hi type="italic">days of the son of man</hi> may wish in vain to see them. And <hi type="italic">in the day</hi> of this famine <hi type="italic">the fair virgins and the young men shall faint for thirst</hi> (<reference osisRef="Amos.8.13">v. 13</reference>); those who, one would think, could well enough have borne the toil, shall sink under it. The <hi type="italic">Jewish churches,</hi> and the <hi type="italic">masters of their synagogues,</hi> some take to be meant by the <hi type="italic">virgins</hi> and the <hi type="italic">young men;</hi> these shall lose the word of the Lord, and the benefit of divine revelation, and shall faint away for want of it, shall lose all their strength and beauty. Those that trust in their own merit and righteousness, and think they have no need of Christ, others take to be meant by the <hi type="italic">fair virgins</hi> and the <hi type="italic">choice young men;</hi> they shall <hi type="italic">faint for thirst,</hi> when those that <hi type="italic">hunger and thirst after the righteousness</hi> of Christ shall be abundantly satisfied and filled. <div eID="gen20240" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20241" type="x-p"/> II. The particular destruction of those that were ringleaders in idolatry, <reference osisRef="Amos.8.14">v. 14</reference>. Observe, 1. The sin they are charged with: They <hi type="italic">swear by the sin of Samaria,</hi> that is, by the god of Samaria, the idol that was worshipped at Bethel, not far off from Samaria. Thus did they glory in their shame, and swear by them as their god which was their iniquity, thinking that could help them which would certainly ruin them, and giving the highest honour to that which they should have looked upon with the utmost abhorrence and detestation. They say, <hi type="italic">Thy god, O Dan! liveth;</hi> that was the other golden calf, a dumb deal idol, and yet caressed and complimented as if it had been the living and true God. They say, <hi type="italic">The manner,</hi> or way, of <hi type="italic">Beer-sheba liveth;</hi> they swore by the <hi type="italic">religion</hi> of Beer-sheba, the way and manner of worship used there, which they looked upon as sacred, and therefore swore by and appealed to as a judge of controversy. Thus the papists swear by the mass, as the <hi type="italic">manner of Beer-sheba.</hi> 2. The destruction they are threatened with. Those who thus give that honour to idols which is due to God alone will find that the God they affront is thereby made their enemy, so that <hi type="italic">they shall fall,</hi> and the gods they serve cannot stand their friends, so that they shall <hi type="italic">never rise again.</hi> They will find that God is jealous and will resent the indignity done him, and that he will be victorious and it is to no purpose to contend with him.  <chapter eID="Amos.8"/> <div eID="gen20241" type="x-p"/>

entries.ef90dc8d7242ca2bdbc36138a4f0ff7c711f798c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12619"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 8</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Amos.8.1-Amos.8.14">Am 8:1-14</reference>. Vision of a Basket of Summer Fruit Symbolical, of Israel's End. Resuming the Series of Symbols Interrupted by Amaziah, Amos Adds a Fourth. The Avarice of the Oppressors of the Poor: The Overthrow of the Nation: The Wish for the Means of Religious Counsel, when There Shall Be a Famine of the Word.</title> <div sID="gen23289" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12619"/><hi type="bold">1. summer fruit--</hi>Hebrew, kitz. In <reference osisRef="Amos.8.2">Am 8:2</reference> "end" is in Hebrew, keetz. The similarity of sounds implies that, as the summer is the end of the year and the time of the ripeness of fruits, so Israel is ripe for her last punishment, ending her national existence. As the fruit is plucked when ripe from the tree, so Israel from her land. <div eID="gen23289" type="x-p"/>
entries.0531ce7933492a6b1e0bc5b0a75c32efe7a5c9ef: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12620"/><div sID="gen23290" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12620"/><hi type="bold">2. end--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ezek.7.2">Eze 7:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.7.6">6</reference>). <div eID="gen23290" type="x-p"/>
entries.d25746422af03956d9d064d1a2b7bf465712b87d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12621"/><div sID="gen23291" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12621"/><hi type="bold">3. songs of ... temple--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Amos.5.23">Am 5:23</reference>). The joyous hymns in the temple of Judah (or rather, in the Beth-el "royal temple," <reference osisRef="Amos.7.13">Am 7:13</reference>; for the allusion is to Israel, not Judah, throughout this chapter) shall be changed into "howlings." Grotius translates, "palace"; compare <reference osisRef="Amos.6.5">Am 6:5</reference>, as to the songs there. But <reference osisRef="Amos.5.23">Am 5:23</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Amos.7.13">Am 7:13</reference>, favor English Version.<div eID="gen23291" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23292" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">they shall cast them forth with silence--</hi>not as the Margin, "be silent." It is an adverb, "silently." There shall be such great slaughter as even to prevent the bodies being buried [Calvin]. There shall be none of the usual professional mourners (<reference osisRef="Amos.5.16">Am 5:16</reference>), but the bodies will be cast out in silence. Perhaps also is meant that terror, both of God (compare <reference osisRef="Amos.6.10">Am 6:10</reference>) and of the foe, shall close their lips. <div eID="gen23292" type="x-p"/>
entries.daf88d1bd38b11fe0a959f60322565fa0c3ab34d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12622"/><div sID="gen23293" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12622"/><hi type="bold">4. Hear--</hi>The nobles needed to be urged thus, as hating to hear reproof.<div eID="gen23293" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23294" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">swallow up the needy--</hi>or, "gape after," that is, pant for their goods; so the word is used, <reference osisRef="Job.7.2">Job 7:2</reference>, Margin.<div eID="gen23294" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23295" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to make the poor ... to fail--</hi>"that they (themselves) may be placed alone in the midst of the earth" (<reference osisRef="Isa.5.8">Is 5:8</reference>). <div eID="gen23295" type="x-p"/>
entries.b9b9a1e52e2fde76519a7a3e02acfe94e12a71c3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12623"/><div sID="gen23296" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12623"/>5. So greedy are they of unjust gain that they cannot spare a single day, however sacred, from pursuing it. They are strangers to God and enemies to themselves, who love market days better than sabbath days; and they who have lost piety will not long keep honesty. The new moons (<reference osisRef="Num.10.10">Nu 10:10</reference>) and sabbaths were to be kept without working or trading (<reference osisRef="Neh.10.31">Ne 10:31</reference>).<div eID="gen23296" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23297" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">set forth wheat--</hi>literally, "open out" stores of wheat for sale.<div eID="gen23297" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23298" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">ephah--</hi>containing three seahs, or above three pecks.<div eID="gen23298" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23299" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">making ... small--</hi>making it below the just weight to purchasers.<div eID="gen23299" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23300" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shekel great--</hi>taking from purchasers a greater weight of money than was due. Shekels used to be weighed out in payments (<reference osisRef="Gen.23.16">Ge 23:16</reference>). Thus they committed a double fraud against the law (<reference osisRef="Deut.25.13">De 25:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.25.14">14</reference>). <div eID="gen23300" type="x-p"/>
entries.fd2621748e47927e1feb2d3e230763b1c678199d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12624"/><div sID="gen23301" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12624"/><hi type="bold">6. buy ... poor for silver ... pair of shoes--</hi>that is, that we may compel the needy for money, or any other thing of however little worth, to sell themselves to us as bondmen, in defiance of <reference osisRef="Lev.25.39">Le 25:39</reference>; the very thing which brings down God's judgment (<reference osisRef="Amos.2.6">Am 2:6</reference>).<div eID="gen23301" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23302" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sell the refuse of ... wheat--</hi>which contains no nutriment, but which the poor eat at a low price, being unable to pay for flour. <div eID="gen23302" type="x-p"/>
entries.d57446dbd28f0b30544c4363a45d09a13a7fa0d9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12625"/><div sID="gen23303" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12625"/><hi type="bold">7. Lord hath sworn by the excellency of Jacob--</hi>that is, by Himself, in whom Jacob's seed glory [Maurer]. Rather, by the spiritual privileges of Israel, the adoption as His peculiar people [Calvin], the temple, and its Shekinah symbol of His presence. Compare <reference osisRef="Amos.6.8">Am 6:8</reference>, where it means Jehovah's temple (compare <reference osisRef="Amos.4.2">Am 4:2</reference>).<div eID="gen23303" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23304" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">never forget--</hi>not pass by without punishing (<reference osisRef="Amos.8.2">Am 8:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.8.13">Ho 8:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.9.9">9:9</reference>). <div eID="gen23304" type="x-p"/>
entries.ca531ee962252eb07ccec4fc87451057cac88c56: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12626"/><div sID="gen23305" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12626"/><hi type="bold">8. the land ... rise up wholly as a flood--</hi>The land will, as it were, be wholly turned into a flooding river (a flood being the image of overwhelming calamity, <reference osisRef="Dan.9.26">Da 9:26</reference>).<div eID="gen23305" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23306" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">cast out and drowned, &c.--</hi>swept away and overwhelmed, as the land adjoining the Nile is by it, when flooding (<reference osisRef="Amos.9.5">Am 9:5</reference>). The Nile rises generally twenty feet. The waters then "cast out" mire and dirt (<reference osisRef="Isa.57.20">Is 57:20</reference>). <div eID="gen23306" type="x-p"/>
entries.0c96344cc475d50efc34ea784c89254302050d25: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12627"/><div sID="gen23307" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12627"/>9. "Darkness" made to rise "at noon" is the emblem of great calamities (<reference osisRef="Jer.15.9">Jr 15:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.32.7-Ezek.32.10">Eze 32:7-10</reference>). <div eID="gen23307" type="x-p"/>
entries.963d973f67e4dffac50982d0b6df8bb073e50ca0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12628"/><div sID="gen23308" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12628"/><hi type="bold">10. baldness--</hi>a sign of mourning (<reference osisRef="Isa.15.2">Is 15:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.48.37">Jr 48:37</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.7.18">Eze 7:18</reference>).<div eID="gen23308" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23309" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I will make it as ... mourning of an only son--</hi>"it," that is, "the earth" (<reference osisRef="Amos.8.9">Am 8:9</reference>). I will reduce the land to such a state that there shall be the same occasion for mourning as when parents mourn for an only son (<reference osisRef="Jer.6.26">Jr 6:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.12.10">Zec 12:10</reference>). <div eID="gen23309" type="x-p"/>
entries.0ac6298b103b9346c372a4a7e019446c855b2167: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12629"/><div sID="gen23310" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12629"/><hi type="bold">11. famine of ... hearing the words of the Lord--</hi>a just retribution on those who now will not hear the Lord's prophets, nay even try to drive them away, as Amaziah did (<reference osisRef="Amos.7.12">Am 7:12</reference>); they shall look in vain, in their distress, for divine counsel, such as the prophets now offer (<reference osisRef="Ezek.7.26">Eze 7:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mic.3.7">Mi 3:7</reference>). Compare as to the Jews' rejection of Messiah, and their consequent rejection by Him (<reference osisRef="Matt.21.43">Mt 21:43</reference>); and their desire for Messiah too late (<reference osisRef="Luke.17.22">Lu 17:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.7.34">Joh 7:34</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.8.21">8:21</reference>). So, the prodigal when he had sojourned awhile in the "far-off country, began to be in want" in the "mighty famine" which arose (<reference osisRef="Luke.15.14">Lu 15:14</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="1Sam.3.1">1Sa 3:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.7.2">7:2</reference>). It is remarkable that the Jews' religion is almost the only one that could be abolished against the will of the people themselves, on account of its being dependent on a particular place, namely, the temple. When that was destroyed, the Mosaic ritual, which could not exist without it, necessarily ceased. Providence designed it, that, as the law gave way to the Gospel, so all men should perceive it was so, in spite of the Jews' obstinate rejection of the Gospel. <div eID="gen23310" type="x-p"/>
entries.53bff2247e59a803bd77b50e67fd878747b45dd7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12630"/><div sID="gen23311" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12630"/><hi type="bold">12. they shall wander from sea to sea--</hi>that is, from the Dead Sea to the Mediterranean, from east to west.<div eID="gen23311" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23312" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">from ... north ... to ... east--</hi>where we might expect "from north to south." But so alienated was Israel from Judah, that no Israelite even then would think of repairing southward, that is, to Jerusalem for religious information. The circuit is traced as in <reference osisRef="Num.34.3">Nu 34:3</reference>, &c., except that the south is omitted. Their "seeking the word of the Lord" would not be from a sincere desire to obey God, but under the pressure of punishment. <div eID="gen23312" type="x-p"/>
entries.f011289b89d183aa8b9392e4c799c668c96ae57b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12631"/><div sID="gen23313" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12631"/><hi type="bold">13. faint for thirst--</hi>namely, thirst for hearing the words of the Lord, being destitute of all other comfort. If even the young and strong faint, how much more the infirm (<reference osisRef="Isa.40.30">Is 40:30</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.40.31">31</reference>)! <div eID="gen23313" type="x-p"/>
entries.f7acf88dac80a1cd7596835d74f873b3d667cafc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12632"/><div sID="gen23314" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12632"/><hi type="bold">14. swear by the sin of Samaria--</hi>namely, the calves (<reference osisRef="Deut.9.21">De 9:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.4.15">Ho 4:15</reference>). "Swear by" means to worship (<reference osisRef="Ps.63.11">Psa 63:11</reference>).<div eID="gen23314" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23315" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">The manner--</hi>that is, as "the way" is used (<reference osisRef="Ps.139.24">Psa 139:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.9.2">Ac 9:2</reference>), the mode of worship.<div eID="gen23315" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23316" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Thy god, O Dan--</hi>the other golden calf at Dan (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.26-1Kgs.22.30">1Ki 22:26-30</reference>).<div eID="gen23316" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23317" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">liveth ... liveth--</hi>rather, "May thy god ... live ... may the manner ... live." Or, "As (surely as) thy god, O Dan, liveth." This is their formula when they swear; not "May Jehovah live!" or, "As Jehovah liveth!" <chapter eID="Amos.8"/>

entries.bb199df8634ff35957b58c85007c640c952217f7: <div eID="gen34448" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen34449" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen34450" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen34450" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen34449" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen34451" type="x-p"/> This chapter begins with a fourth vision denoting the certainty and nearness of the destruction of Israel, <reference osisRef="Amo.8.1-Amo.8.3">Amo 8:1-3</reference>. The prophet then proceeds to reprove their oppression and injustice, <reference osisRef="Amo.8.4-Amo.8.7">Amo 8:4-7</reference>. Strong and beautiful figures, by which is represented the complete dissolution of the Israelitish polity, <reference osisRef="Amo.8.8-Amo.8.10">Amo 8:8-10</reference>. The people threatened with a most awful judgment; a Famine of the word of God, <reference osisRef="Amo.8.11-Amo.8.14">Amo 8:11-14</reference>. <div eID="gen34451" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34452" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen34452" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34453" type="x-p"/> A basket of summer fruit - As summer fruit was not proper for preserving, but must be eaten as soon as gathered, so the Lord intimates by this symbol that the kingdom of Israel was now ripe for destruction, and that punishment must descend upon it without delay. Some think the prophet means the fruits at the end of autumn. And as after the autumn no fruit could be expected, so Israel's summer is gone by, her autumn is ended, and she shall yield no more fruit. Or, the autumn of her iniquity is come, the measure is filled up, and now she shall gather the fruit of her sin in the abundance of her punishment.
entries.93ac28a0fdc74b633f92a862378203b7640aef9b: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen34453" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34454" type="x-p"/> A basket of summer fruit - כלוב קיץ kelub kayits, the end is come - בא הקץ ba hakkets: here is a paronomasia or play upon the words kayits, summer fruit, and kets, the end, both coming from similar roots. See the note on <reference osisRef="Eze.7.2">Eze 7:2</reference> (note), where there is a similar play on the same word. <div eID="gen34454" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34455" type="x-p"/> I will not again pass by them any more - I will be no longer their Guardian.
entries.afd0b4d95625b19ce548d1b85df16f26a53e045f: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen34455" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34456" type="x-p"/> The songs of the temple - Instead of שירות shiroth, songs, Houbigant reads שורות shoroth, the singing women; and Newcome follows him: "And the singing women of the palace shall howl in that day." Instead of joyous songs, they shall have nothing but lamentation. <div eID="gen34456" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34457" type="x-p"/> They shall cast them forth with silence - Every place shall be filled with the dead, and a dreadful silence shall reign universally; the few that remain being afraid either to speak or complain, or even to chant a funeral dirge for the most respectable of the dead.
entries.62c6c5a6c33f48e3465ffed2cdcf507a557bb3fb: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen34457" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34458" type="x-p"/> Hear this, O ye that swallow up the needy - Ye that bruise the poor; exact from them, and tread them under foot.
entries.aa23aae03ede2849f9d4c413cedecd82251a6e87: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen34458" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34459" type="x-p"/> When will the new moon be gone - This was kept as a kind of holy day, not by Divine command, but by custom. The Sabbath was strictly holy; and yet so covetous were they that they grudged to give to God and their own souls this seventh portion of time! But bad and execrable as they were, they neither set forth their corn, nor their wheat, nor any other kind of merchandise, on the Sabbath. They were saints then, when compared to multitudes called Christians, who keep their shops either partially or entirely open on the Lord's day, and buy and sell without any scruples of conscience. Conscience! alas! they have none; it is seared as with a hot iron. The strong man armed, in them, is quiet, for all his goods are in peace. <div eID="gen34459" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34460" type="x-p"/> Making the ephah small, and the shekel great - Giving short measure, and taking full price; or, buying with a heavy weight, and selling with one that was light. <div eID="gen34460" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34461" type="x-p"/> Falsifying the balances - Having one scale light, and the other weighty; one end of the beam long, and the other short. A few months ago I detected a knave with such balances; with a slip of his finger along the beam he altered the center, which made three ounces short weight in every pound. He did it so dexterously, that though I knew he was cheating, or, as the prophet expresses it, was falsifying the balances by deceit, it was some time before I could detect the fraud, and not till I had been several times cheated by this accomplished knave. So we find that though the knaves of ancient Israel are dead, they have left their successors behind them.
entries.affb50261704d3e29477c6ee7b1caf7478b5f49d: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen34461" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34462" type="x-p"/> That we may buy the poor for silver - Buying their services for such a time, with just money enough to clear them from other creditors. <div eID="gen34462" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34463" type="x-p"/> And the needy for a pair of shoes - See <reference osisRef="Amo.2.6">Amo 2:6</reference>. <div eID="gen34463" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34464" type="x-p"/> And sell the refuse of the wheat! - Selling bad wheat and damaged flour to poor people as good, knowing that such cannot afford to prosecute them.
entries.60c082b5a3e132d3fe5595f5d623cc4292de4eec: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen34464" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34465" type="x-p"/> By the excellency of Jacob - By the state of eminence to which he had raised the descendants of Jacob; or, by the excellent One of Jacob, that is, Himself. The meaning is: "As surely as I have raised you to such a state of eminence, so surely will I punish you in proportion to your advantages and your crimes."
entries.df0fb3a62b3a12613848224518bb5376d4294e67: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen34465" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34466" type="x-p"/> Shall not the land tremble for this - It is supposed that an earthquake is here intended, and that the rising up and subsiding as a flood refers to that heaving motion that takes place in an earthquake, and which the prophet here compares to the overflowing and subsiding of the waters of the Nile. But it may refer to commotions among the people.
entries.963f4d83eabf1deae60a69f1a216b73f95973b46: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen34466" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34467" type="x-p"/> I will cause the sun to go down at noon - This may either refer to that darkness which often precedes and accompanies earthquakes, or to an eclipse. Abp. Usher has shown that about eleven years after Amos prophesied there were two great eclipses of the sun; one at the feast of tabernacles, and the other some time before the passover. The prophet may refer to the darkness occasioned by those eclipses; yet I rather think the whole may refer to the earthquake.
entries.04a9905da8b55ae42f55bf123019b7eb2511d812: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen34467" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34468" type="x-p"/> I will turn your feasts into mourning - See on <reference osisRef="Amo.8.3">Amo 8:3</reference> (note). <div eID="gen34468" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34469" type="x-p"/> A bitter day - A time of grievous calamity.
entries.2fb39372846463f46e838bf026e24f11b8ff9fce: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen34469" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34470" type="x-p"/> A famine in the land - The most grievous of all famines, a famine of the words of Jehovah; a time in which no prophet should appear, no spiritual counsellor, no faithful reprover, none any longer who would point out the way of salvation, or would assure them of the mercy of God on their repentance and return to him. This is the severest of God's judgments on this side the worm that never dieth, and the fire that is never quenched.
entries.d0ac9aeccc881bdbe37632c51b61fd6d7596027d: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen34470" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34471" type="x-p"/> They shall wander front sea to sea - From the Mediterranean to the Dead Sea or from west to east, and from north to south, to seek the word of the Lord; to find a prophet, or any person authorized by God to show them the end of their calamities. In this state they shall continue, because they have rejected Him who is the bread of life.
entries.902431ebb1560e8624f8129f82e6dd8f4c2b336f: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen34471" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34472" type="x-p"/> By the sin of Samaria - Baal, who was worshipped here. <div eID="gen34472" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34473" type="x-p"/> Thy god, O Dan - The golden calf, or ox, the representative of the Egyptian god Apis, or Osiris. <div eID="gen34473" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34474" type="x-p"/> The manner of Beer-sheba - The worship, or object of worship. Another of the golden calves which Jeroboam had set up there. The word דרך derech, way, is here taken for the object and mode of worship; see <reference osisRef="Act.19.9">Act 19:9</reference>, where way is taken for the creed and form of Divine worship as practiced by the followers of Christ, and by which they were distinguished from the Jews. See also <reference osisRef="Act.9.2">Act 9:2</reference>.  <chapter eID="Amos.8"/> <div eID="gen34474" type="x-p"/>

entries.55e19c438550ca72df06b379d2137fdb648d4e4a: <div eID="gen16415" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">The Ripeness of Israel for Judgment - <reference osisRef="Amos.8.1-Amos.8.14">Amo 8:1-14</reference></title> <div sID="gen16416" type="x-p"/> Under the symbol of a basket filled with ripe fruit, the Lord shows the prophet that Israel is ripe for judgment (<reference osisRef="Amos.8.1-Amos.8.3">Amo 8:1-3</reference>); whereupon Amos, explaining the meaning of this vision, announces to the unrighteous magnates of the nation the changing of their joyful feasts into days of mourning, as the punishment from God for their unrighteousness (<reference osisRef="Amos.8.4-Amos.8.10">Amo 8:4-10</reference>), and sets before them a time when those who now despise the word of God will sigh in vain in their extremity for a word of the Lord (<reference osisRef="Amos.8.11-Amos.8.14">Amo 8:11-14</reference>).
entries.ce050346837696b372728b623fdd9efdc93c9749: <reference osisRef="Amos.8.1-Amos.8.3">Amo 8:1-3</reference> <div eID="gen16416" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16417" type="x-p"/> Vision of a Basket of Ripe Fruit. - Amo 8:1. <hi type="italic">“Thus did the Lord Jehovah show me: and behold a basket with ripe fruit.</hi> Amo 8:2. <hi type="italic">And He said, What seest thou, Amos? And I said, A basket of ripe fruit. Then Jehovah said to me, The end is come to my people Israel; I will not pass by them any more.</hi> Amo 8:3. <hi type="italic">And the songs of the palace will yell in that day, is the saying of the Lord Jehovah: corpses in multitude; in every place hath He cast them forth: Hush!” </hi>כּלוּב from כּלך, to lay hold of, to grasp, lit., a receiver, here a basket (of basket-work), in <reference osisRef="Jer.5.27">Jer 5:27</reference> a bird-cage. קיץ: summer-fruit (see at <reference osisRef="2Sam.16.1">2Sa 16:1</reference>); in <reference osisRef="Isa.16.9">Isa 16:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.28.4">Isa 28:4</reference>, the gathering of fruit, hence ripe fruit. The basket of ripe fruit (<hi type="italic">qayits</hi>) is thus explained by the Lord: the end (<hi type="italic">qēts</hi>) is come to my people (cf. <reference osisRef="Ezek.7.6">Eze 7:6</reference>). Consequently the basket of ripe fruit is a figurative representation of the nation that is now ripe for judgment, although <hi type="italic">qēts</hi>, the end, does not denote its ripeness for judgment, but its destruction, and the word <hi type="italic">qēts</hi> is simply chosen to form a paronomasia with <hi type="italic">qayits</hi>. לא אוסיף וגו as in Amo 7:8. All the joy shall be turned into mourning. the thought is not that the temple-singing to the praise of God (<reference osisRef="Amos.5.23">Amo 5:23</reference>) would be turned into yelling, but that the songs of joy (<reference osisRef="Amos.6.5">Amo 6:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.19.36">2Sa 19:36</reference>) would be turned into yells, i.e., into sounds of lamentation (cf. <reference osisRef="Amos.8.10">Amo 8:10</reference> and 1 Maccabees 9:41), namely, because of the multitude of the dead which lay upon the ground on every side. השׁליך is not impersonal, in the sense of “which men are no longer able to bury on account of their great number, and therefore cast away in quiet places on every side;” but Jehovah is to be regarded as the subject, viz., which God has laid prostrate, or cast to the ground on every side. For the adverbial use of הס cannot be established. The word is an interjection here, as in <reference osisRef="Amos.6.10">Amo 6:10</reference>; and the exclamation, Hush! is not a sign of gloomy despair, but an admonition to bow beneath the overwhelming severity of the judgment of God, as in Zep 1:7 (cf. <reference osisRef="Hab.2.20">Hab 2:20</reference> and Zec 2:13).
entries.f2a818a0248e0ecbb56e9dd8616f7ba127b4219f: <reference osisRef="Amos.8.4-Amos.8.6">Amo 8:4-6</reference> <div eID="gen16417" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16418" type="x-p"/> To this vision the prophet attaches the last admonition to the rich and powerful men of the nation, to observe the threatening of the Lord before it is too late, impressing upon them the terrible severity of the judgment. Amo 8:4. <hi type="italic">“Hear this, ye that gape for the poor, and to destroy the meek of the earth,</hi> Amo 8:5. <hi type="italic">Saying, When is the new moon over, that we may sell corn? and the sabbath, that we may open wheat, to make the ephah small, and the shekel great, and to falsify the scale of deceit?</hi> Amo 8:6. <hi type="italic">To buy the poor for silver, and the needy for a pair of shoes, and the refuse of the corn will we sell.” </hi> The persons addressed are the השּׁאפים אביון, i.e., not those who snort at the poor man, to frighten him away from any further pursuit of his rights (Baur), but, according to <reference osisRef="Amos.2.6-Amos.2.7">Amo 2:6-7</reference>, those who greedily pant for the poor man, who try to swallow him (Hitzig). This is affirmed in the second clause of the verse, in which שׁאפים is to be repeated in thought before להשׁבּית: they gape to destroy the quiet in the land (ענוי־ארץ = ענוים, in <reference osisRef="Amos.2.7">Amo 2:7</reference>), “namely by grasping all property for themselves, <reference osisRef="Job.22.8">Job 22:8</reference>; Isa 5:8” (Hitzig). <reference osisRef="Amos.8.5">Amo 8:5</reference> and <reference osisRef="Amos.8.6">Amo 8:6</reference> show how they expect to accomplish their purpose. Like covetous usurers, they cannot even wait for the end of the feast-days to pursue their trade still further. <hi type="italic">Chōdēsh</hi>, the new moon, was a holiday on which all trade was suspended, just as it was on the Sabbath (see at Num 28:11 and 2Ki 4:23). השׁבּיר שׁבר, to sell corn, as in Gen 41:57. פּתח בּר, to open up corn, i.e., to open the granaries (cf. <reference osisRef="Gen.41.56">Gen 41:56</reference>). In doing so, they wanted to cheat the poor by small measure (ephah), and by making the shekel great, i.e., by increasing the price, which was to be weighed out to them; also by false scales (<hi type="italic">‛ivvēth</hi>, to pervert, or falsify the scale of deceit, i.e., the scale used for cheating), and by bad corn (<hi type="italic">mappal</hi>, waste or refuse); that in this way they might make the poor man so poor, that he would either be obliged to sell himself to them from want and distress (<reference osisRef="Lev.25.39">Lev 25:39</reference>), or be handed over to the creditor by the court of justice, because he was no longer able to pay for a pair of shoes, i.e., the very smallest debt (cf. <reference osisRef="Amos.2.6">Amo 2:6</reference>).
entries.f1d31629390f22fa4855e8b4c139e985b3151210: <reference osisRef="Amos.8.7-Amos.8.8">Amo 8:7-8</reference> <div eID="gen16418" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16419" type="x-p"/> Such wickedness as this would be severely punished by the Lord. Amo 8:7. <hi type="italic">“Jehovah hath sworn by the pride of Jacob, Verily I will not forget all their deeds for ever.</hi> Amo 8:8. <hi type="italic">Shall the earth not tremble for this, and every inhabitants upon it mourn? and all of it rises like the Nile, and heaves and sinks like the Nile of Egypt.” </hi> The pride of Jacob is Jehovah, as in Hos 5:5 and Hos 7:10. Jehovah swears by the pride of Jacob, as He does by His holiness in <reference osisRef="Amos.4.2">Amo 4:2</reference>, or by His soul in <reference osisRef="Amos.6.8">Amo 6:8</reference>, i.e., as He who is the pride and glory of Israel: i.e., as truly as He is so, will He and must He punish such acts as these. By overlooking such sins, or leaving them unpunished, He would deny His glory in Israel. שׁכח, to forget a sin, i.e., to leave it unpunished. In <reference osisRef="Amos.8.8">Amo 8:8</reference> the negative question is an expression denoting strong assurance. “For this” is generally supposed to refer to the sins; but this is a mistake, as the previous verse alludes not to the sins themselves, but to the punishment of them; and the solemn oath of Jehovah does not contain so subordinate and casual a thought, that we can pass over <reference osisRef="Amos.8.7">Amo 8:7</reference>, and take על זאת as referring back to <reference osisRef="Amos.8.4">Amo 8:4</reference>-6. It rather refers to the substance of the oath, i.e., to the punishment of the sins which the Lord announces with a solemn oath. This will be so terrible that the earth will quake, and be resolved, as it were, into its primeval condition of chaos. <hi type="italic">Râgaz</hi>, to tremble, or, when applied to the earth, to quake, does not mean to shudder, or to be shocked, as Rosenmüller explains it after Jer 2:12. Still less can the idea of the earth rearing and rising up in a stormy manner to cast them off, which Hitzig supports, be proved to be a biblical idea from Isa 24:20. The thought is rather that, under the weight of the judgment, the earth will quake, and all its inhabitants will be thrown into mourning, as we may clearly see from the parallel passage in Amo 9:5. In <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Amos.8.8">Amo 8:8</reference></hi> this figure is carried out still further, and the whole earth is represented as being turned into a sea, heaving and falling in a tempestuous manner, just as in the case of the flood. כּלּהּ, the totality of the earth, the entire globe, will rise, and swell and fall like waters lashed into a storm. This rising and falling of the earth is compared to the rising and sinking of the Nile. According to the Parallel passage in <reference osisRef="Amos.9.5">Amo 9:5</reference>,  כּאר  is a defective form for  כּיאר,  just as  בּוּל  is for  יבוּל  in <reference osisRef="Job.40.20">Job 40:20</reference>, and it is still further defined by the expression  כּיאור מצרים,  which follows. All the ancient versions have taken it as יאור, and many of the Hebrew codd. (in Kennicott and De Rossi) have this reading. Nigrash, to be excited, a term applied to the stormy sea (<reference osisRef="Isa.57.20">Isa 57:20</reference>). נשׁקה is a softened form for נשׁקעה, as is shown by שׁקעה in Amo 9:5.
entries.c9cfb9d575cd0319de832ed4c39933e64e3d5eba: <reference osisRef="Amos.8.9-Amos.8.10">Amo 8:9-10</reference> <hi type="italic">“And it will come to pass on that day, is the saying of the Lord Jehovah, I cause the sun to set at noon, and make it dark to the earth in clear day.</hi> Amo 8:10. <hi type="italic">And turn your feasts into mourning, and all your songs into lamentation: and bring mourning clothes upon all loins, and baldness upon every head; and make it like mourning for an only one, and the end thereof like a bitter day.” </hi> The effect of the divine judgment upon the Israelites is depicted here. Just as the wicked overturn the moral order of the universe, so will the Lord, with His judgment, break through the order of nature, cause the sun to go down at noon, and envelope the earth in darkness in clear day. The words of the ninth verse are not founded upon the idea of an eclipse of the sun, though Michaelis and Hitzig not only assume that they are, but actually attempt to determine the time of its occurrence. An eclipse of the sun is not the setting of the sun (כּוא). But to any man the sun sets at noon, when he is suddenly snatched away by death, in the very midst of his life. And this also applies to a nation when it is suddenly destroyed in the midst of its earthly prosperity. But it has a still wider application. When the Lord shall come to judgment, at a time when the world, in its self-security, looketh not for Him (cf. Mat 24:37.), this earth’s sun will set at noon, and the earth be covered with darkness in bright daylight. And every judgment that falls upon an ungodly people or kingdom, as the ages roll away, is a harbinger of the approach of the final judgment. Amo 8:10. When the judgment shall burst upon Israel, then will all the joyous feasts give way to mourning and lamentation (compare <reference osisRef="Amos.8.3">Amo 8:3</reference> and <reference osisRef="Amos.5.16">Amo 5:16</reference>; Hos 2:13). On the shaving of a bald place as a sign of mourning, see Isa 3:24. This mourning will be very deep, like the mourning for the death of an only son (cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.6.26">Jer 6:26</reference> and Zec 12:10). The suffix in שׂמתּיה (I make <hi type="italic">it</hi>) does not refer to אבל (mourning), but to all that has been previously mentioned as done upon that day, to their weeping and lamenting (Hitzig). אחריתהּ, the end thereof, namely, of this mourning and lamentation, will be a bitter day (כ is <hi type="italic">caph verit.</hi>; see at <reference osisRef="Joel.1.15">Joe 1:15</reference>). This implies that the judgment will not be a passing one, but will continue.
entries.52c48bc47715a9b36caa596bf14bad4d95495e95: <reference osisRef="Amos.8.11-Amos.8.12">Amo 8:11-12</reference> <div eID="gen16419" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16420" type="x-p"/> And at that time the light and comfort of the word of God will also fail them. Amo 8:11. <hi type="italic">“Behold, days come, is the saying of the Lord Jehovah, that I send a hungering into the land, not a hungering for bread nor a thirst for water, but to hear the words of Jehovah.</hi> Amo 8:12. <hi type="italic">And they will reel from sea to sea; and from the north, and even to the east, they sweep round to seek the word of Jehovah, and will not find it.”</hi> The bitterness of the time of punishment is increased by the fact that the Lord will then withdrawn His word from them, i.e., the light of His revelation. They who will not now hear His word, as proclaimed by the prophets, will then cherish the greatest longing for it. Such hunger and thirst will be awakened by the distress and affliction that will come upon them. The intensity of this desire is depicted in Amo 8:12. They reel (נוּע as in <reference osisRef="Amos.4.8">Amo 4:8</reference>) from the sea to the sea; that is to say, not “from the Dead Sea in the east to the Mediterranean in the west,” for <reference osisRef="Joel.2.20">Joe 2:20</reference> and Zec 14:8 are not cases in point, as the two seas are defined there by distinct epithets; but as in <reference osisRef="Ps.72.8">Psa 72:8</reference> and Zec 9:10, according to which the meaning is, from the sea to where the sea occurs again, at the other end of the world, “the sea being taken as the boundary of the earth” (Hupfeld). The other clause, “from the north even to the east,” contains an abridged expression for “from north to south and from west to east,” i.e., to every quarter of the globe.
entries.3de85292e5669b48dc2f8168ec3ba6757f7e126e: <reference osisRef="Amos.8.13-Amos.8.14">Amo 8:13-14</reference> <hi type="italic">“In that day will the fair virgins and the young men faint for thirst.</hi> Amo 8:14. <hi type="italic">They who swear by the guilt of Samaria, and say, By the life of thy God, O Dan! and by the life of the way to Beersheba; and will fall, and not rise again.” </hi> Those who now stand in all the fullest and freshest vigour of life, will succumb to this hunger and thirst. The virgins and young men are individualized, as comprising that portion of the nation which possessed the vigorous fulness of youth. עלף, to be enveloped in night, to sink into a swoon, <hi type="italic">hithp.</hi> to hide one’s self, to faint away. הנּשׁבּעים refers to the young men and virgins; and inasmuch as they represent the most vigorous portion of the nation, to the nation as a whole. If the strongest succumb to the thirst, how much more the weak! <hi type="italic">'Ashmath Shōmerōn</hi>, the guilt of Samaria, is the golden calf at Bethel, the principal idol of the kingdom of Israel, which is named after the capital Samaria (compare <reference osisRef="Deut.9.21">Deu 9:21</reference>, “the sin of Israel”), not the Asherah which was still standing in Samaria in the reign of Jehoahaz (2Ki 13:6); for apart from the question whether it was there in the time of Jeroboam, this is at variance with the second clause, in which the manner of their swearing is given, - namely, by the life of the god at Dan, that is to say, the golden calf that was there; so that the guilt of Samaria can only have been the golden calf at Bethel, the national sanctuary of the ten tribes (cf. <reference osisRef="Amos.4.4">Amo 4:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amos.5.5">Amo 5:5</reference>). The way to Beersheba is mentioned, instead of the worship, for the sake of which the pilgrimage to Beersheba was made. This worship, again, was not a purely heathen worship, but an idolatrous worship of Jehovah (see <reference osisRef="Amos.5.5">Amo 5:5</reference>). The fulfilment of these threats commenced with the destruction of the kingdom of Israel, and the carrying away of the ten tribes into exile in Assyria, and continues to this day in the case of that portion of the Israelitish nation which is still looking for the Messiah, the prophet promised by Moses, and looking in vain, because they will not hearken to the preaching of the gospel concerning the Messiah, who appeared as Jesus. Destruction of the Sinful Kingdom, and Establishment of the New Kingdom of God - <reference osisRef="Amos.9.1-Amos.9.15">Amo 9:1-15</reference> <div eID="gen16420" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16421" type="x-p"/> The prophet sees the Lord standing by the altar, and giving command to overthrow the temple, that the whole nation may be buried beneath the ruins (<reference osisRef="Amos.9.1">Amo 9:1</reference>). Should any one escape, the Lord will pursue him everywhere, and overtake and destroy him (<reference osisRef="Amos.9.2-Amos.9.4">Amo 9:2-4</reference>); for He is the Almighty God, and the Judge of the world (<reference osisRef="Amos.9.5">Amo 9:5</reference> and <reference osisRef="Amos.9.6">Amo 9:6</reference>); and Israel has become like the heathen, so that it deserves no sparing. Nevertheless it shall not be utterly destroyed, but simply sifted, and the sinful mass be slain (<reference osisRef="Amos.9.7-Amos.9.10">Amo 9:7-10</reference>). Then will the fallen tabernacle of David be raised up again, and the kingdom of God be glorified by the reception of all nations (<reference osisRef="Amos.9.12">Amo 9:12</reference>), and richly blessed with the fulness of the gifts of divine grace (<reference osisRef="Amos.9.13">Amo 9:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Amos.9.14">Amo 9:14</reference>), and never destroyed again (<reference osisRef="Amos.9.15">Amo 9:15</reference>). As the chapter gives the final development of the judgment threatened in the preceding one, so is it also closely attached in form to ch. 7 and <reference osisRef="Amos.8.1-Amos.8.14">Amo 8:1-14</reference>, commencing with a vision just as they do. But whilst the preceding visions simply indicate the judgment which is to fall upon the sinful nation, and are introduced with the words, “The Lord showed me” (<reference osisRef="Amos.7.1">Amo 7:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Amos.7.4">Amo 7:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Amos.7.7">Amo 7:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amos.8.1">Amo 8:1</reference>), this closing vision shows the Lord engaged in the execution of the judgment, and commences accordingly with the words, “I saw the Lord standing,” etc.  <chapter eID="Amos.8"/> <div eID="gen16421" type="x-p"/>

entries.5a30db7df231729d03e6173d7b200b0ea7d1253d: <div annotateRef="Bible:Amos.8.1" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Amos.8.1" sID="gen85044" type="section"/> <div sID="gen85045" type="x-p"/>By these words or by this vision the Prophet confirms what we have already observed — that paternal chastisements would no longer be exercised towards the people of Israel. God indeed, as it is well known, had so treated that people, that he ever spared them even in their greatest calamities. It was with a suspended hand that God ever struck that people, until after many trials they at length seemed so refractory, as not to be benefited by such remedies. This subject then Amos now pursues: but a vision was shown to him to confirm more fully God’s judgment, or at least to produce a greater impression on the minds of the people.<div eID="gen85045" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen85046" type="x-p"/>God showed to him a <hi type="italic">Basket</hi> full of summer-fruit. By summer-fruit, I doubt not, he means a ripe punishment, as though he said, that the vices of the people had ripened, that vengeance could no longer be deferred: for an exposition of the vision immediately follows, when he says, that <hi type="italic">the end of the people had come, etc.</hi>; and this we have already explained in the third vision. But there is a similarity in the Hebrew words, which cannot be expressed either in Greek or Latin. <foreign xml:lang="he">קיץ</foreign>, <hi type="italic">kits</hi> means a summer-fruit, <foreign xml:lang="he">קץ</foreign>, <hi type="italic">kots,</hi> signifies an end: one letter only is inserted in the word, summer-fruit, which God showed in a basket; and then he adds that <foreign xml:lang="he">קץ</foreign>, <hi type="italic">kots</hi>, the end had come. But as to the main point, we see that there is nothing ambiguous. We will now return to the first thing.<div eID="gen85046" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen85047" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">Thus God showed to me.</hi> There is no need of repeating what I have already discussed. The Prophet here prefaces, that he adduced nothing without authority, but only faithfully related what had been commanded him from above. And this ought to be carefully observed; for God ever so employed his Prophets, that he yet reserved for himself entire the right of teaching, and never transferred his own office to men, that is, as to the authority. Then he says, <hi type="italic">The Lord Jehovah showed to me, and, lo, a basket of summer-fruit.</hi> We may understand cherries by summer-fruit, and those fruits which have no solid vigor to continue long; but this is too refined. I take the simple meaning, that punishment had now become ripe; for the people had not repented, though they had been so often warned; it was then as it were summer. He showed to me a basket of summer-fruit. But as to God asking his Prophet what he saw, we have already explained the reason why it was done: it behaved the Prophet to be at first filled with astonishment, that the people might be made more attentive; for when we hear of a conference between God and the Prophet, our minds are awakened; inasmuch as it must immediately occur to us, that there is something worthy of being remembered. God then rouses in this manner the minds of his people. So we see there is nothing superfluous in this repetition.<div eID="gen85047" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Amos.8.1" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen85044" osisID="Amos.8.1" type="section"/>
entries.753ebed1d614844738e4068b509f764e91fad4dd:
Now follows the exposition of the vision, Jehovah said to me, Come has the end on my people Israel We perceive, then, the meaning of the Prophet to be, — that the people had hitherto been warned by moderate punishments; but that as they had become hardened, extreme vengeance was nigh at hand, when God would no longer perform the part of a father or of a physician, but would utterly destroy those whom he had long borne with.
